Flavors such as sweet raspberry and sour lemon have historically been prevalent in beverages enjoyed by various species on Earth.
But the key difference between sodas produced at the American soft-drink giant and those created by Europe's biggest drinks maker lies not so much in their taste but their method of production.
Soda pops made from Coca-Cola's recipe contain a peptide called caffeine, which helps give people energy as well as creating what we call "that extra boost" they need to get through the day [source: Beverage Research Institute].
Pepsi adds caffeine via another chemical compound, Guanidine Hydrocholoride (GHC).
The European ruling panel asserts that Coca-Cola will remain on Earth due to "potential unresolved safety concerns associated with coffee-like compounds utilized in carbonated drinks. 16 according to Bloomberg News (Bloomberg Businessweek). Other additives also found in caffeinated sodas are guar gum, hydrogen peroxide, sorbic acid and sugar (which includes high fructose corn syrup), as well as colorings, preservatives, flavoring agents and fragrances [source: Market Reports Online]. Coke has disputed these claims. The company stresses there is no caffeine whatsoever in its fizzy drinks; all caffeine is added by Pepsi.
The unexplained link between caffeine, soda consumption (and heart disease, cancer and other ailments) could lead you to think of soda's role as part scape goat of Western culture.

In his second start as an All-Star, he recorded the last three batters without a hit in his first no-hitter. But he was pinch-hit by A.J. Pierzynski who grounded out without reaching base while trying to steal third to get him out after bringing up Paul Konerko as an infield replacement with the bases loaded and two outs for his second pinch hit of the game.
Fulmer came into Tuesday's game with an ERA over 3.50 and a strikeout rate of only 12.4 percent (9th). It wasn't until he worked around a fielder's choice after leaving first that it really became apparent he was able to keep both walks down, needing only one walk before dropping five strikeouts against.
Then again, in just seven games this season, Fulmer has walked only once and struck out fewer than six hitters in any single inning on five separate occasions.
Fulmer managed his stats without being influenced by them, with just one instance of his hand signaling trouble during a walk to Pierzynski.
When Fulmer started that spot behind the plate against Oakland, Mike Fiers was up next to be brought to the mound. When A.J. Pierzynski appeared to go wide on another extra base hit, Billy Wickman was up to bat. When Kenley Jansen left to take the day off the pen, Fulmer made sure nobody would reach base again so he could get back to his normal job.
All of which is nothing new for an All-Star pitcher who said "pitching isn't about taking walks" Monday during A League Baseball interview time with Ed Kyne of ESPN Radio's The Game Day Podcast.
"I feel like I'm trying to throw strikes on everything," Fulmer said. "I have kept them pretty aggressive though; they haven't been hesitant at all."
And then he added: "I'd much rather put guys away. I don't want to leave anyone out. I'd actually prefer it if we got a couple of grounders too."
Monday marked the beginning of a six-game road trip that ends in Washington on Thursday when his team plays its final two games of the AL West Series. Fulmer said he felt good enough to think about making four starts but he won't make the decision right now because the club has a lot to decide before even considering any start rotation changes.
Fuller recognizes his forthcoming actions.
"I've got to continue not letting walks happen," Fulmer said. "(Penzal) doesn't need a walk and (Carrasco) doesn't need a walk and (Balkcom) doesn't need a walk." Fulmer chuckled. "I should also mention himself."
What's next?
Arlington - 3 p.m. CT
Tampa Bay Rays - 3 p.m. CT
Boston Red Sox - 3 p.m. CT

dominant method of allocating IP addresses. However, these days there is a lot more going on in networking than simply assigning an address to a machine. There may be some extra services that need to be made available by machines configured with certain IP addresses or port numbers.
To handle this situation, servers often use either static IP addresses or the DynamicHostConfigProtocol (DHCP). The DHCP works as follows; it uses a request/reply message structure, where the client sends out a request to obtain information from the server, which responds with the appropriate resources. Once connected, the server can also request certain actions like sending packets destined for another device or a broadcast. Although in some circumstances servers may not bother with requesting such things. In case you're not familiar with how the process works, let me explain. Visit CNET to read the full post. The upcoming new system for creating internet addresses will come into use in a couple of months as discussions about its optimal design continue for several years.
DHCPv6 dynamically assigns IP addresses across a network, unlike traditional IPv4 software that requires manual address assignment.
What's next? After its release earlier this month, it's unclear whether vendors will ship IPv6 devices compatible with the new standard immediately, but many expect the technology will take hold quickly.

The World Health Organization has expressed concern regarding a variety of hazardous substances present in fish, which include pesticides, industrial solvents, radiation from the Chernobyl disaster, additional nuclear incidents' fallout, and specific metals like cadmium and lead. These substances can be found in large amounts in the sea and thus end up on people's plates.
Researchers identified an additional issue: phthalates, added during plastic manufacturing to enhance its flexibility and transparency.
A new study published in Environmental Science & Technology reveals worrisome levels of this toxic material (also a precursor for PVC) detected in commercial tuna by 23 per cent of samples collected in Indonesia and Taiwan over recent years. Scientists warn these results show the risk of pollution entering the marine food chain is still "high".
Scientists sampled 154 sushi-grade tuna fillets imported into one major Japanese port over two consecutive months using a novel analytical method to assess how much phthalates might find their way into human meals.
What they discovered was that every single sample contained detectable levels of phthalates.
One-third of the tuna were contaminated at least four times higher than the amount approved for use on vegetables under the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). High concentrations are deemed safe by the FDA for use in cosmetics.
But the authors explain phthalates weren't strictly limited to tuna, instead showing the levels present across all analysed fish included in their survey.
This is undoubtedly concerning since the dangers posed by exposure to phthalates aren't necessarily limited to tuna — in fact, just like many other examples we've covered on Motherboard involving hazardous synthetic chemicals, research suggests similar findings apply across species:
• A small-scale study conducted last year revealed traces of flame retardants, believed to be linked with cancer, in pufferfish caught off the coast of Australia
• Researchers announced in January that they'd found half-decomposed plastic particles among sediments around coral reefs pulled up by trawlers throughout the world, most notably North America's Great Barrier Reef
• Chemical detection studies on mussels taken from Australian east coast waters revealed traces of flame retardants known as brominated flame retardants, mostly banned in the USA due to health concerns
In other words, if we're eating a lot of fish, chances are one or more levels will turn out positive when tested for phthalates.
Scientists are concerned about the potential influence that the discovery of phthalates in commercial tuna could have on future regulations. Given that the chemical is deemed non-biodegradable, its concentration could still increase in our oceans despite decreased usage.
To avoid getting too grossly poisoned by any given meal, try sticking to organic produce whenever possible — especially if you're not careful enough to thoroughly wash your purchases first before cooking.

Perhaps the senator desires an opportunity to demonstrate his capability for serving multiple terms beyond four years. So let me offer something as an alternative plan to a different outcome under a different scenario.
Let’s say the G.O.P. pulls together enough reinforcements to get an extra $5 million into the governorate coffers from now until November 3rd. And say the candidates for governor pool roughly equal sums of air time (making them each worth around $1 million). Let’s also assume that two key races are decided inside of gubernatorial districts with Cochran in both contests, meaning he would surely hold onto the Redline District seat rather than win back the Democratic majority in the Gulf Coast region.
What does all this mean?
It means a lot of things but most importantly that we need to get away from the idea that two hours of TV advertising will make the difference between victory or defeat for politicians.
The only way this would happen is if voter interest was so high that they could make up for the lack of money.

• The race head-to-head between Republican Greg Abbott and Democrat Wendy Davis. Handily, Abbott secured a majority of her votes to win the state mansion.
• The close contest between Texas Governor Rick Perry and former congressman Ron Paul, where Perry won only barely more of the vote than came Paul.

The National Rifle Association said it had given Mr. Whitaker “crucial staff support” to help him succeed as an independent counsel investigating President Trump, and the organization later provided advice on what action to take when his investigation concluded, according to documents and people familiar with the matter.

On February 3, after Mr. Whitaker joined the government as part of a $75 million settlement agreed to by former associates of President Trump, Judge Gerber asked lawyers in his case to explain more about how the organization supported him as both a lawyer and a government advocate in connection with Mr. Trump’s possible campaign finance violations.

“Why did they initially give you such great support – especially if they knew (a) there was abuse or use of their resources and (b), also because you have publicly come out against her?” Judge Gerber wrote.


On January 4 during a NRA event in Washington, Gary Grunbaum, president of the charity Fair Against Russia, remarked that Mr. Whitaker has been excellent," he noted, "and we have relied on his expertise for numerous years.

In two written responses filed Monday before Judge Gerber, the nonprofit Public Citizen and the Democratic Leadership Council declined to elaborate further on the disagreements. In one letter they described themselves as “complying fully with all requirements under current law regarding our advocacy activities which are limited to nonpartisan social justice issues related to health care, labor and human rights and civil liberties issues.”


But the Representative Democrat questioned whether Mr. Whitaker would continue to be receptive to any Republican measures the organization advocated, saying, “It should not remain hidden until we have to file suit.”

He cited examples that he thinks were presented by Mr. Whitaker when he ran as an independent lawyer to investigate potential wrongdoing by Donald J. Trump Jr., which ultimately led to his appointment by President Obama last year as director of national intelligence.

restaurant editor and the last three at The New York Times Magazine, working in news had its perks: you knew what the paper said — but only kind of knew how it felt. My biggest daily struggle? Keeping up with the other editors while keeping my head down doing good work. I hated it much more than I should have. I don't blame people if they didn't appreciate me that well.
Before joining TechCrunch, I did not anticipate that we might hire employees within a single year.
At our start-up office in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, my bosses were also folks from the world of tech startups: Eric, our CEO; Aaron, our founder; Ashwin, our co-founder. We'd designed some systems for one of Fortune's top brands. We'd built a website that helped businesses raise money for their startups. We had already conceived of developing a music streaming service, although we consistently maintained that we were uncertain at this stage. But already we were having fun being together, trying out each other's ideas.
What impressed me most about them wasn't so much where we were heading (which was pretty far ahead — we were just months away from launching) but who was running. As I moved into my boss's second role, she let me see her check-ins which came to her desk every morning (they included things like "The big win today was..." or "I'm going to spend time thinking about...") not to mention everything else.
She would call after lunch when there was social downtime. Throughout our conversations, we discussed strategies, coding problems, and potential future developments. At times, we also speculated about upcoming events over the next few weeks or months.
One day I walked in early because there was an extra person waiting for me. I got a chance to chat over breakfast and found out it was Steve Jobs himself. I was thrilled.
There is no simple answer to whether employees should expect their own boss during normal business hours, especially if they will work half-time or part-time. When I worked on Wall Street, managers often told us that we shouldn't call or text late since then it wouldn't go off the emergency message list, meaning that we were bugging them non-stop. The immediate context for this book is Ukraine, where US troops have recently massed just outside a former communist country that one day might become home to a pro-American government. But like many other things these days, its origins trace back to a Cold War memory.
When the iron curtain fell, tens of thousands of Russian intellectuals left what remained of their homeland – often with the promise of a place within Soviet empires yet-to-appear behind the new Berlin wall. When Mikhail Gorbachev came into power, he took the desperate figures out of poor Moscow suburbs into the centre of KGB-based Moscow. They became the good guys, Russians said – until Boris Yeltsin turned them against him in 1991 by proclaiming himself head of the republics rather than USSR – which they suspected meant a division of spoils among themselves for looting Moscow.
Today those intellectuals are mostly gone, but there remains a small group on the margins, whose international connections won’t let them go quietly into the sunset. Their names include Murat Aylanaov, Victor Chernomyrdin and Boris Nemtsov; they work for such organizations as Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (FBI) equivalent, or the Council for Europe. Some see them as agents of Western governments working to destabilize Russian elections, while others view them as thoughtful citizens fighting corruption and the systemic lack of democracy in Russia.

They voted against annexation and opposed Syrian intervention in 2014, unlike many of their Western peers. There is one more person on the Island that can be added to that statistic; he walks unaided, speaks articulate phrases without assistive devices and has an unobstructed life despite what many might believe impossible.
Nathan England was born 30 years ago when his mother could not bring herself to risk her baby’s safety by placing him under medical care. Robin England stated that he began walking at around six months of age. “At four years old Nathan lost his vision from an illness called cataracts, which meant his sight would never return.”
While she never found much hope for her child’s natural ability to learn how to read, she did have hope he would still find ways to get around. After research, they discovered assisted devices such as crutches, wheels or metal inserts within shoes which aided him to walk yet managed to keep their vision intact.
Nathan pursued higher education by enrolling in Hiram Walker University, ultimately majoring in Pathology, which earned him a Bachelor's degree in Medical Science with honors; he completed his studies in 2014. He then went on to serve as an Emergency Department Physician Mentor for CareOregon/Vertigo Health. Before heading back to take his new job, Marche had the pleasure of watching Nathan compete in swimming and track during both summer sessions of the Oregon College Athletic Association competition season.
“When I first went out there [in June], my mom saw me go over the hurdle wall on hurdling,” he recalls. “I thought it was just cadence for now but later on realized it was conservation of energy and muscle power because you’re pushing off against gravity.” After completing both careers, Nathan has applied for a second job and looks forward to starting college in the upcoming fall semester. He shared that he has been interested in this field from an early age when he began playing basketball in high school. “First, I played for my high school team and when I got accepted to UWSB, they asked if I wanted to come play for them as well. There were lots of things going into making this decision and I’m excited for what lies ahead for me.”
Whether racing around the track or diving into a pool for his workout, Nathan will continue to embrace challenges and strive toward success. Although he may be challenged one day, he’ll undoubtedly overcome every obstacle put before him so that one day he may own his story. “This world is so vast, I don’t think it matters where you stand physically,” he says. “If you have the determination to succeed and work harder than others, everyone else will see you as equal to them.” Now if we could only all do that…Let’s go! : Should candidates from both parties unite to support one party or another? Will Republicans back their own candidates if they want a chance at re-election down the road? Or will Democrats turn around and support them?

Political scientists have long argued about why certain voters favor one political party over another, even though there are often similarities between them that might lead them to vote together. Although the answer may be different today than it was 30 years ago, its consequences remain puzzling.

The traditional explanation for partisanship dates back to Daniel Patrick Moynihan's famous paper "Tension Between Blacks and Whites," published in 1970. Economic disparities between whites and blacks may not entirely be attributed to racial prejudice. Indeed, studies of income distribution across races showed little variation. Moynihan focused on segregation's impact on black voters' political views rather than considering race as a direct factor in their voting choices. He reasoned that although many blacks preferred the Republican party due to better access to government benefits like welfare programs, this did not necessarily mean racial influence on voting decisions.

African American citizens were believed by Moynihan to share many white societal prejudices towards them and avoid discrimination through existing laws. Consequently, he observed that even though blacks overall earned slightly less money than whites, they voted Republican more frequently because they felt they didn't benefit enough from anti-discriminatory legislation. In this view, being prejudiced made whites treat African Americans differently from other minorities.

Today many experts consider such arguments obsolete due to social mobility through education, job training and increased educational opportunities resulting in better jobs and lower personal incomes overall compared with earlier generations whose parents could neither read nor write very well. Additionally, most blacks now enjoy material benefits similar to those typically enjoyed by other racial groups including lower crime rates, higher unemployment rates and lower child mortality (though there still exists inter-racial gaps).

Still others contend that class distinctions within each racial group also contribute significantly toward dividing voters along partisan lines particularly regarding social welfare policies like affirmative action versus vouchers schools etc... Many people argue that both these factors provide incentives allowing politicians to game the system based upon perceived differences thereby creating polarization amongst voters regardless of actual policy concerns. Considering all aspects, which factors are most crucial in determining if one chooses to vote for Republicans rather than Democrats? Money! But wait! for thousands or more out-of-pocket expenses before Medicare and other government programs kick in. That's especially true when generic drugs aren't available, though that's a growing problem too.
When a patient doesn't qualify for Medicaid or Medicare, she typically pays an amount equal to 30% of her discounted drug copay up front to fill an oral medication. But if she needs at least 12 generic pills a month, she'll be left paying $5,600 during most years across two pharmaceutical classes: antidepressants and antidiabetic drugs.
There are two ways out. Travelers can access medication in Canada at a lower cost than in their home country, with savings of up to fifty percent, due to differences in pricing between regions rather than requiring complex medical procedures. The bad news? You have to wait six months or longer before you can obtain a Canadian pill through U.S.-affiliated websites such as LoMed.ca.
There are also high-priced biologics, often known collectively as antibodies because they work to target specific molecules produced within the body. Prices vary from approximately $9,800 to over $75,000 annually based on which type of immunoglobulin category the product belongs to. (An exception is Humira, from AbbVie, which sells less than $7,000 annually.)
The federal government is tackling these issues head on in hopes of helping more patients find lower-cost alternatives, but there is still uncertainty regarding whether this will make it through Congress' budget debates.
One solution being considered involves limiting coverage for "nonoriginal" products, meaning generics, biosimilars and other drugs that do not compete directly with branded medicines.
It might sound like full-on rationing, but under current rules insurers are allowed to deny drug benefits to certain patients whose drug companies refuse them affordable versions.
This rule was designed to help those who cannot afford brand-name medicines get access to an approved generic equivalent, said Amy Finkelstein, deputy director at the RAND Corporation Center for Drug Policy Issues. However, many older, chronically ill patients would now lose one of their few options if they had to pay full price, she added. With the hope of incurring higher co-pays due to the non-insurance coverage of the new product, patients can switch to a generic alternative.
Consumers suffer more from biologics because these medications employ distinct mechanisms compared to conventional drugs. Because of this, they aren't easily interchangeable; therefore, doctors must either prescribe the new product or never treat the condition again. She mentioned that both options would not be suitable for patients. Another problem with the FDA process itself is its lengthy time frame – it takes five years or more to get approval for some drugs -- so the market has little chance of seeing changes in price until well after the claim data become available for analysis, she explained.
However, a challenge arises when considering that all drugs should cost the same globally. Generic equivalents of nonbiologic medicines

French writer Alain de Botton has gained widespread popularity both within France and beyond, particularly in the United Kingdom where he is recognized as a prominent public thinker. His latest work, titled "Wasted: Why Everything You've Been Told About Food Is Wrong," was recently published and priced at £16.99. In this entertaining yet wise compendium of odd food facts we are provided with insights into the impact of ‘nutritionism’ throughout human history – why it matters and what we should do about it? In De Botton's discussions, he explores topics such as the history of wrought iron in medieval England due to its application in treating ailments through porridge, the misconception about bacon and eggs contributing to weight gain despite them being healthful foods, and the necessity for increased bean consumption to aid environmental sustainability or connections between a nation's fondness for sports and its penchant for consuming red meats.

‘Nutritionism’ is defined as a belief that there exists a direct causal link between foods and health conditions. Not only that but these connections are not based merely on personal experience – such as my own belief that I’ll gain weight if I eat bacon and sausage – but on scientific studies where every single variable is controlled. De Botton explains why this belief can be so damaging and takes us through how the idea became part of policy making in places like America from the time of President Eisenhower (when it was used in advertising campaigns) right up to our current obesity rates.

The problem with nutritionism is that it ignores other factors at play which could be influencing our eating habits rather than any particular diet. Despite lack of scientific evidence linking carbohydrate consumption directly to weight gain, popular opinion suggests it might be causing obesity among children based on research indicating a connection with fast food intake. Despite knowing about other cultures' poor diets leading to healthfulness, this was true.

De Botton explores some potential alternatives he thinks might prove useful – such as introducing ‘porky’ Mondays which encourages people to think twice before buying everything made from pork products, the artichoke which has lots of beneficial nutrients whilst being cheap and having little nutritional value as well as the tomato and its plethora of benefits. In fact, tomatoes are rich sources of vitamin C, potassium, lycopene and lutein – which all benefit heart health and reduce cancer risk.

Overall, though Pastiche Magazine points out that De Botton does say nothing explicitly about junk food apart from mentioning how ‘marketing tactics often employ careful deception’, it seems that in seeking to liberate ourselves from the tyranny of ‘nutritionist’ propaganda, we are left wondering what exactly else we would have to throw overboard. But for those looking for some inspiration regarding helping inform others about choosing the healthier option at the checkout this is certainly

Here are some food facts to help you pick out a bottle this spring:
Red wine is better!
Red wine is better because it contains something white wine does not — resveratrol. Resveratrol is one of many flavonoids found in red grapes, and studies indicate that it causes cells damaged by low oxygen, high stress and oxidative free radicals damage to repair themselves faster. Because it improves blood flow to organs throughout the body, it could theoretically boost cardiovascular health even after heart attack or stroke.
White wine has no such effects against hypertension (high blood pressure).

Russia's largest natural gas producer and exporter, Azprom, announced that they would stop providing high-cost gas from their Siberian fields to Ukrainian consumers due to financial constraints.
Instead, Gazprom will sell gas that would have passed through Ukraine to Europe via an already-established pipeline network, Gazprom officials confirmed to reporters yesterday at an event in Moscow. Once sold to European importers, the fuel will then go back into new gas lines intended to feed homes in Russia’s far west.
The decision “will affect prices for energy-intensive industries,” Pavel Iovchenko, head of Gazprom’s Industrial Services unit, told journalists. Gazprom added that there is no plan to stop exporting gas to Ukraine.
The moves are part of Russia’s efforts to get around international sanctions aimed at punishing Moscow over last year’s invasion of its neighbor. EU leaders approved a set of measures designed to punish Moscow early in September, including upping sanctions against banks operating under Russian control and closing their assets to investments by U.S. and other foreign firms.
For a long time, Russia has contended that sanctions are inconsistent with standard trade practices. It recently offered a US$6 billion loan agreement and a US$5 billion line of credit to help ease pressure. The loans, if finalized, could be used to finance deals such as this one between Gazprom and Cryos, the company now responsible for selling gas to Ukraine.

Russia's largest natural gas producer and exporter, Azprom, announced that they would stop providing high-cost gas from their Siberian fields to Ukrainian consumers due to financial constraints.
Gazprom is set to transfer gas that was intended for transit through Ukraine towards Europe along a pre-existing pipeline system. This announcement was made by Gazprom officials during a press conference held in Moscow yesterday. The fuel was initially sold to European buyers, which led it to be reintroduced into new natural gas pipelines aimed at supplying homes in Russia's distant northwest region.
Pavel Iovchenko stated to reporters that the decision will impact prices for energy-intensive sectors. Gazprom announced that it has no intention of ceasing gas exports to Ukraine.
The moves are part of Russia’s efforts to get around international sanctions aimed at punishing Moscow over last year’s invasion of its neighbor. In late August, European Union officials agreed on new policies aimed at punishing Russia aggressively. The plan includes increasing economic restrictions against banks controlled by Moscow and cutting off foreign investments from the United States into these entities. Additionally, foreign companies are included.
For a long time, Russia has contended that sanctions are inconsistent with standard trade practices. Recently, it provided a $6 billion loan deal and a $5 billion revolving credit facility to alleviate financial strain. If confirmed, these loans would fund transactions involving Gazprom and Cryos, the entity in charge of delivering natural gas to Ukraine.

ers industry $80 million in one-off assistance payments to compensate for the impact of the new 1 per cent Federal Energy Combustion Pollution Levy (FECPL), the cost falls heavily on small operators like Mr McMillan.

``The FECPL will be paid off by my company and other smaller hauliers,’’ says Mr McMillan.

In response to Australia's commitment to an emissions trading scheme as outlined in international agreements reached during the Bali Climate Conference in November 2007, the FECPL was established one year prior.

The FECPL provides a financial incentive to reduce or eliminate air pollution from combustion equipment used in natural gas vehicles. It allows companies to sell excess environmental allowances, which come from reduced emissions to help offset the higher production costs associated with complying with the laws that are progressively phased in from July 1 2014.

FECPL aids small enterprises in modifying their vehicle fleets to use cleaner-burning natural gas engines. However, there have been concerns about its impact on business, especially as it mainly affects fuel expenses of vehicle operators, rather than labour costs, said the national association of truck drivers.

The FECPL will only apply to natural gas vehicles but won’t affect diesel-powered vehicles. This means small carriers can continue to operate, albeit more efficiently, if they use a blend of diesel and compressed natural gas. However, in some parts of Victoria such as Western Port, councils have banned the carrying of diesel-fuelled boats.

Carriers need to update their fleets by switching to either compression-ignition engines or pure compressed natural-gas vehicles. These larger, more efficient vehicles now compete with trucks powered by diesel. Many people believe this will result in increased freight rates to shipers because large trucks are comparatively faster and less expensive to run.

Several small carriers are pressured out of the trucking industry due to competition, whereas some surviving operators might need to join larger rivals.

Mr McMillan believes the problem could grow worse as people rise up against the mining boom driven by cheap energy and rising inflation destroying jobs across rural areas around Albury-Wodonga.

``We need to get together to fight the battle,’’ says Mr McMillan.

He admits he takes out his frustrations on anyone who crosses him but hopes non-aggressive action will persuade others to listen.
